title: ulams — Frequently asked questions
description: Answers about ULAMS: headless LMS, course generation from sources, AI and data, self-hosting, integrations, academies and sales.
heading: Frequently asked questions
intro: What ULAMS is, how courses are built from your sources, what self-hosting takes, and how it connects to the rest of your stack.

items.q: What is ULAMS and who is it for?
items.a: ULAMS is an open-source LMS for creating and delivering courses. It helps teams turn product documentation, manuals and internal material into training for customers, developers and employees.

items.q: What does “headless LMS” mean? Do I have to build my own frontend?
items.a: Headless means the content and features of the platform are available through an API, independently of the user interface. You can use the interface that ships with ULAMS or build your own learning experience inside your application.

items.q: Can I try ULAMS before installing it?
items.a: Yes. The site has demos you can open as a learner and as an administrator, with no account. The demo environments are reset regularly, so they are not a place to keep your own material.

items.q: Do I need to know how to code to use ULAMS?
items.a: Authors create and manage courses in the admin panel and the Studio. Installing and running your own environment needs technical knowledge. You need to code only if you want to build your own frontend, extend the platform or prepare a custom integration.

items.q: How is ULAMS different from other LMSs?
items.a: ULAMS combines a backend available through an API, self-hosting, and optional course creation from your sources under the author’s control. You can use the ready-made interface or design your own. This helps most when learning is part of your product and you need control over integrations, data and how courses are presented.

items.q: Is ULAMS a good choice for every organisation?
items.a: It works best where integrations, your own infrastructure or a custom learning experience matter. Self-hosting means you are responsible for configuration, updates and maintenance. If you need a fully managed service, first decide who will take care of those tasks.

items.q: What material can I build a course from?
items.a: The Course Builder accepts Markdown, PDF and DOCX documents. Material with a clear structure and real text works best; a scanned PDF without a text layer needs text recognition first. The default limit is 20 MB per file and 300 pages per PDF. You can also connect a Git repository, a Google Drive file or folder or a Notion page; the Drive and Notion connectors are off until an administrator turns them on.

items.q: What do the source references in a generated course mean?
items.a: References let you check the fragment of the document a lesson or question is based on. ULAMS checks generated lessons against the cited fragments and flags content that needs attention. This makes review easier, but it does not replace the author’s judgement.

items.q: Can AI publish a course without my approval?
items.a: In the Course Builder the author approves the course structure and every proposed change. A course is first created unpublished, and publishing is a separate step. You can check the preview and edit the content before learners see it.

items.q: What happens when my documentation changes?
items.a: Living Course compares source versions and points to the parts of the course that may need an update. You can upload a new version of the document or connect a Git repository, a Google Drive file, a Notion page or a website. Changes to the course need the author’s decision: a new source version never overwrites published content on its own. Learner Insights can also turn a section many learners struggle with into an improvement proposal, which you review the same way.

items.q: Are my documents sent to an external AI provider?
items.a: When you use AI generation, the fragments of your material needed for the task are sent to the configured model service. The current Course Builder uses Claude through the Anthropic API. Self-hosting the platform does not mean the AI model runs locally. You can turn AI features off and keep using the rest of the LMS.

items.q: Can I use ULAMS without AI?
items.a: Yes. AI is optional. You can create courses by hand, add material, manage learners and access, and track progress. Turning AI off does not disable any other LMS feature and does not require a model provider key.

items.q: How do I review what the AI changed?
items.a: Every AI change, whether it comes from generation, a chat edit, a source update or a learner-insights proposal, arrives as a diff: what is removed, what is added and the passage behind it. You accept it all, accept element by element or reject it, and the audit trail records who approved what and when. Nothing reaches learners without approval, and version history lets you undo to an earlier version.

items.q: Can one course have versions for different levels and roles?
items.a: Yes, in the Course Builder. The interview can ask for a beginner, intermediate or expert version and for roles you name. Each is drafted from the same sources, reviewed as a diff against the base course and approved one by one into its own unpublished course. Sending each learner to the right version is not built yet: today an administrator enrols learners in a variant by hand.

items.q: Can I see what changed between two versions of a course?
items.a: Partly. Every apply is recorded as a numbered release, listed in the studio, and you can compare any two versions or releases through the API, the command line or an AI agent. The studio screen that shows the comparison side by side is not built yet.

items.q: How were the numbers on this site measured?
items.a: They come from single runs of the real Studio with a real model, and each is labelled as one run. A public docs repository of 13 passages became 6 lessons and 18 quiz questions in 7 min 44 s of generation, for USD 0.28. A Notion page of 6 passages took 27 s for the outline, 4 min 58 s for lessons, quizzes and checks and 1 s to apply, for USD 0.1973. Times and costs are copied from the Studio’s own records. Author review comes on top, one run on a small source says nothing about large ones, and we claim no speed-up ratio.

items.q: Which modules and features does ULAMS support?
items.a: Courses and content: courses, lessons, text, video, audio, images, PDF and embedded material. Interactive content: H5P, SCORM, cmi5, LiaScript, quizzes and project assignments. Users and access: accounts, groups, roles, permissions and course access. Assessment and reporting: results, progress, reports and PDF certificates. Organising learning: webinars, consultations, in-person events, notifications, notes and bookmarks. Sales: payments, cart and coupons. Creating and maintaining content: the Course Builder and Living Course. Integrations and many academies: REST API, developer tools and tenants. What is available in a given interface depends on the version, configuration and connected services.

items.q: Can I reuse my existing SCORM courses and interactive content?
items.a: Yes. ULAMS accepts SCORM 1.2 and SCORM 2004 packages and supports H5P content and cmi5 packages. You can combine them with other material in a course. Before going live, test your own packages, playback and progress tracking in the target environment.

items.q: Can I move material and users from my current LMS?
items.a: ULAMS imports SCORM packages and imports and exports courses in the .ulam format. There is also a module for importing and exporting users as CSV. Moving other data, such as progress history or purchases, needs a compatibility check and a prepared migration. Importing material does not recreate the full history of the previous platform.

items.q: Is the learner interface accessible?
items.a: Learner-facing pages are built to WCAG 2.2 AA: keyboard navigation, visible focus, text alternatives and reduced motion. Automated accessibility checks run in the test suite. If you build your own frontend, accessibility of that interface is up to you.

items.q: Can I run ULAMS on my own infrastructure?
items.a: Yes. ULAMS runs on your own server in containers. The documentation describes configuring the application, domains, mail, file storage and backups. A production deployment needs configuration and testing in the environment you choose.

items.q: What do I need to install ULAMS?
items.a: A standard deployment needs a server with 64-bit Linux, Docker Engine and Docker Compose v2. You also need a domain with DNS and HTTPS, storage for course files and an SMTP service for sending email. The installation guide covers each of them. An AI provider key is needed only if you want content generation.

items.q: How powerful does the server need to be?
items.a: The documentation suggests about 2 vCPU, 4 GB RAM and 40 GB SSD for tests with a few users, and 4 vCPU, 8 GB RAM and 80 GB SSD for a small production deployment. These are estimates, not a performance guarantee. Needs depend on concurrent users, package imports and video processing; plan storage for course material separately.

items.q: Can I try the whole stack locally?
items.a: Yes. Install the CLI and run ulams stack up with Docker Compose available. The development trial uses deterministic AI responses without paid model calls. Node.js 22.12 or newer is required.

items.q: Where can I deploy it?
items.a: Use Docker Compose on your own server or native Kubernetes manifests on an existing cluster. A VPS or virtual machine on AWS, Google Cloud or Azure can host the stack. Production needs DNS, HTTPS and persistent storage.

items.q: How do I stop it without losing courses?
items.a: Run ulams stack down. Data and credentials remain available when you run stack up again in the same installation directory. Only stack down --purge --yes deliberately removes persistent data.

items.q: How much does ULAMS cost?
items.a: The platform code is open source under the MIT licence. When you self-host, you pay for infrastructure, maintenance and any external services you use. AI generation is billed by the model provider; ULAMS shows generation costs and lets you set budget limits. Some components have their own licences, described in the documentation; H5P runs as a separate service under the GPL.

items.q: How do I upgrade to a new version?
items.a: Back up the database and files first, then follow the upgrade steps for your deployment in the documentation. The upgrade runs database migrations for the platform and every academy. Check the release notes for changes that need configuration before you upgrade production.

items.q: Where are course files stored when I self-host?
items.a: In S3-compatible storage with one bucket per academy. The bundled SeaweedFS store gives every academy its own key limited to its bucket, so one academy’s key cannot list, write or delete another’s files; a file whose exact name is known stays readable, as the public-read policy intends. An external S3 service such as AWS S3 or Cloudflare R2 works with one shared key, but the project does not test provider accounts. Images are resized by the built-in service or, as a deployment choice, by Cloudflare Image Transformations. A script moves an existing MinIO installation over.

items.q: Can I connect ULAMS to my own application or a Python backend?
items.a: Yes. Integration goes through the REST API, so your application can be written in Python or any language that speaks HTTP. ULAMS also provides OpenAPI documentation, an SDK, a CLI and an MCP interface. Fit the scope of the integration, including sign-in and course access, to the architecture of your application.

items.q: Can agents operate ULAMS?
items.a: The CLI and MCP interface let compatible agents work with the platform. You can use Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or Gemini CLI, or integrate directly through the REST API.

items.q: Can I extend ULAMS with my own features?
items.a: Yes. The platform is modular and the source code is open. You can build your own API modules, content types, interface components and integrations. The documentation includes guides and a sample extension module.

items.q: Can I keep a course in Git and edit it as code?
items.a: In part. The command line can write a course as a folder of Markdown and YAML, then show status and differences, pull, push, apply and publish. When both the folder and the server changed, it merges element by element and writes conflicts to files you resolve. Not built yet: a GitHub Action, a preview academy for each pull request, a Git merge that triggers a Living Course proposal, and courses that were not made with the Course Builder.

items.q: Can I run several academies on one installation?
items.a: Yes. ULAMS supports many academies, called tenants. Each can have its own addresses, database, file storage, accounts and theme, so you can run separate environments for customers, brands or departments. Creating and maintaining them is done by the platform operator. Today each academy has its own subdomain; a subdomain or entry point for each course or role inside one academy is not built.

items.q: Can I match an academy to my brand?
items.a: Yes. An academy can have its own name, theme, accent colour, logo and domain. The admin theme screen checks the accent colour’s contrast against WCAG 2.2 AA and does not save one that fails. For deeper changes you can extend the frontend that ships with ULAMS or build your own interface on the ULAMS API.

items.q: Can I sell access to courses?
items.a: The platform includes modules for prices, payments, cart and coupons, and every access grant is recorded as an entitlement with its source. Selling needs a supported payment gateway to be configured and the whole flow tested, from purchase to granting access. Which sales scenarios are available depends on the version and interface you use.

items.q: Does ULAMS support single sign-on?
items.a: Learners can sign in with Google or Facebook, and each academy can connect its own identity provider through OpenID Connect or SAML 2.0. Providers are set up through the API or the command line. There is no admin screen yet, SAML sign-in has to start at ULAMS rather than at the provider, groups and roles are not mapped and SCIM provisioning is not built. SAML was tested against Keycloak; Entra ID and Okta are documented but not run by the project.

items.q: Where can I get help?
items.a: Start with the documentation. For questions about self-hosting, integrations or a project, use the contact form on the main page. Bugs and feature requests go to the issue tracker on GitHub.

items.q: How can I contribute?
items.a: ULAMS is developed in the open on GitHub. You can report issues, suggest changes to the documentation and send pull requests. The contributing section of the documentation explains how the code is organised and how changes are reviewed.
